name: Chi Lăng Pass
summary: A narrow valley on the old road from China to Thăng Long. For a thousand years, Vietnamese armies ambushed invaders here.

eras.label: Long ago
eras.title: A natural trap
eras.text: The valley of Chi Lăng is several kilometres long and only a few hundred metres wide in places, hemmed in by limestone cliffs and the Thương River. An army marching through it is stretched out and easy to attack from the hills.

eras.title: Lê Hoàn's ambush
eras.text: When a Song army invaded from the north, the Vietnamese ruler Lê Hoàn lured its land forces into the Chi Lăng valley and defeated them. The Song general Hầu Nhân Bảo was killed.

image.alt: The valley floor at Chi Lăng

eras.title: The fall of Liễu Thăng
eras.text: In 1427 a large Ming relief army marched south to save the Ming troops besieged by Lê Lợi. In the hills around Chi Lăng, Vietnamese forces ambushed it and killed its commander, Liễu Thăng. Within months the Ming withdrew, ending twenty years of occupation.

image.file: Tuong dai chien thang Chi Lang.JPG

eras.label: Today
eras.title: Memory in the valley
eras.text: Today a monument and temples stand in the valley, and the railway and highway to the border run past them. The name Chi Lăng is a byword in Vietnam for a place where invaders were defeated.

story.title: The ambush of 1427

image.file: Tuong dai chien thang Chi Lang.JPG

story.narration: By 1427, Lê Lợi's army had trapped the Ming forces in the citadels of the delta. The Ming emperor sent a huge relief army south through Lạng Sơn under General Liễu Thăng. Lê Lợi's commanders waited in the hills. They drew the advance guard into the narrow valley, and near Mã Yên mountain they killed Liễu Thăng and scattered his troops. The rest of the relief army was defeated soon after. Within months the Ming commanders agreed to leave, and the next year Lê Lợi founded the Lê dynasty.

story.title: The Gate of Ghosts
story.narration: On the old road north there was a pass known as Quỷ Môn Quan, the Gate of Ghosts. An old saying warned that of ten men who went through it, only one would come back. For Chinese soldiers and officials marching south, it marked the start of a dangerous, malaria-ridden land. For Vietnamese, it was a reminder that the mountains themselves had defended the country.

story.title: The woman who waited
story.narration: In Lạng Sơn city, a rock on a mountainside is said to be a woman holding her child. The legend says that her husband went off to war and never came back. Every day she climbed the mountain with her baby to watch the road, until both slowly turned to stone. Her name was Tô Thị. The rock fell in 1991 and was later restored, and the story is still told to visitors as a symbol of faithfulness.

guide.price: Free to visit the valley and monument.

hours.notes: The monument area is open; small temples nearby open in the daytime.

do: Combine Chi Lăng with Lạng Sơn city on the drive to the border.
Use a local guide to find the old battle sites.

tips.title: Lạng Sơn food
tips.text: Roast pork with mắc mật leaves, and phở chua (sour phở) are local favourites.

tips.title: Getting there
tips.text: About 2 hours from Hà Nội on the expressway to Lạng Sơn; trains on the Hà Nội–Đồng Đăng line pass through Chi Lăng.

tips.title: Nearby
tips.text: In Lạng Sơn city: the Tam Thanh and Nhị Thanh caves, and the Kỳ Lừa night market.
